title: ArrayList vs LinkedList — when to use each
shortTitle: ArrayList vs LinkedList — when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: `ArrayList` = backed by a **dynamic array**. O(1) random access by index (`get(i)`), O(1) amortized `add()` at end, but O(n) insert/remove in the middle (shifts elements). `LinkedList` = **doubly-linked list** where each node holds a reference to the previous and next node. O(1) add/remove at head/tail, but O(n) random access (`get(i)` must traverse from head/tail). In practice: **ArrayList wins 95% of the time** — CPU cache locality (contiguous memory) makes it faster even for operations that are theoretically slower. LinkedList is only better for frequent add/remove at both ends (use as Deque) or when you hold a `ListIterator` and insert/remove at the iterator position.
s1_definition.analogy: **ArrayList** = bank's account ledger in a BOOK (numbered pages). Finding account #500? Flip to page 500 instantly (O(1)). Adding a new account at the END? Write on the next blank page (fast). Inserting an account in the MIDDLE? Rewrite all subsequent pages to shift them (slow). **LinkedList** = bank's accounts on STICKY NOTES chained together. Adding/removing at either end? Stick/unstick one note (fast). Finding account #500? Follow the chain from note 1 → 2 → 3... → 500 (slow).
s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList = array, O(1) get, cache-friendly, best default. LinkedList = linked nodes, O(1) add/remove ends, O(n) get. Use ArrayList unless you specifically need a Deque.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ArrayList` = backed by a **dynamic array**. O(1) random access by index (`get(i)`), O(1) amortized `add()` at end, but O(n) insert/remove in the middle (shifts elements). `LinkedList` = **doubly-linked list** where each node holds a reference to the previous and next node. O(1) add/remove at head/tail, but O(n) random access (`get(i)` must traverse from head/tail). In practice: **ArrayList wins 95% of the time** — CPU cache locality (contiguous memory) makes it faster even for operations that are theoretically slower. LinkedList is only better for frequent add/remove at both ends (use as Deque) or when you hold a `ListIterator` and insert/remove at the iterator position.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **ArrayList** = bank's account ledger in a BOOK (numbered pages). Finding account #500? Flip to page 500 instantly (O(1)). Adding a new account at the END? Write on the next blank page (fast). Inserting an account in the MIDDLE? Rewrite all subsequent pages to shift them (slow). **LinkedList** = bank's accounts on STICKY NOTES chained together. Adding/removing at either end? Stick/unstick one note (fast). Finding account #500? Follow the chain from note 1 → 2 → 3... → 500 (slow).

**One line to remember:** ArrayList = array, O(1) get, cache-friendly, best default. LinkedList = linked nodes, O(1) add/remove ends, O(n) get. Use ArrayList unless you specifically need a Deque.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The transaction history service used LinkedList** because "we add transactions frequently." But the UI paged through transactions with `get(offset)` — O(n) for each page request. With 100K transactions: page 100 required traversing 10K nodes. Fix: switched to ArrayList — `get(offset)` is O(1), and `add()` at end is also O(1). Page load time: 200ms → 0.1ms.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the same transactions stored in an `ArrayList` and a `LinkedList`.

**Step 1.** The `ArrayList` stores elements in a contiguous backing array, so `get(index)` for Rajesh's balance is a direct O(1) lookup.

**Step 2.** The `LinkedList` stores elements as chained nodes, so the same `get(index)` must walk the chain in O(n), but inserting at the head is O(1).

**Step 3.** For read-heavy, index-based access the ArrayList wins, while for frequent front or middle insertions the LinkedList is the better fit.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ArrayList (dynamic array) ═══

  Internal: [A][B][C][D][E][_][_]   (contiguous memory)
  get(2) → array[2] → "C"  O(1)!
  add("F") → array[5] = "F"  O(1)!
  add(0,"Z") → shift ALL right → O(n)!

  ═══ LinkedList (doubly-linked) ═══

  first → [A] ⇄ [B] ⇄ [C] ⇄ [D] ← last
  get(2) → A → B → C  O(n)! (traverse)
  addFirst("Z") → [Z] ⇄ [A] ⇄ ...  O(1)!
  addLast("E") → ... ⇄ [D] ⇄ [E]  O(1)!

  ═══ DECISION ═══
  Need random access (get/set by index)?     → ArrayList ✅
  Mostly add/iterate?                         → ArrayList ✅
  Need Deque (addFirst/removeLast)?           → ArrayDeque > LinkedList
  Insert/remove during iteration (Iterator)?  → LinkedList ✅
  Default choice?                             → ArrayList (95% of cases)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array — O(1) random access, O(1) amortized add at end, O(n) insert/remove in the middle. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list — O(1) add/remove at head/tail, but O(n) random access (must traverse nodes). In practice, ArrayList wins 95% of the time because of CPU cache locality — contiguous memory means the CPU prefetches efficiently, making even O(n) shifts faster than LinkedList's O(n) traversal (pointer chasing causes cache misses).

LinkedList uses ~6x more memory than ArrayList (each node = object header + item + prev + next pointers = ~24 bytes vs ArrayList's ~4 bytes per element reference). Use ArrayList as default. Use LinkedList ONLY as a Deque (but ArrayDeque is even better). The only true LinkedList advantage: O(1) insert/remove at the current position during iteration with ListIterator — useful for algorithms that modify the list while traversing. In banking: transaction history → ArrayList (paginated access by index). Transaction processing queue → ArrayDeque (FIFO). Never LinkedList for random access.
